case_studies.title: SkillGate: Cost Efficient Runtime Malicious Skill File Detection in Coding Agents
case_studies.abstract: Software engineering teams now deploy AI coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot) as first-class productivity tools, installing domain-specific skill files to tailor agent behavior to project APIs, framework conventions, and organizational workflows. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of malicious skill files in AI coding agents by building a cost-efficient detection system called SkillGate, which successfully detects and prevents attacks. The result is a more secure coding environment for software engineering teams. This affects IT infrastructure work related to cloud-based coding tools and AI-powered development.

case_studies.title: Agent Skills Matter: Inferring Proprietary Skills from Execution Trajectories
case_studies.abstract: Agent skills package reusable procedures that improve downstream performance. Their lightweight, portable form enables marketplace monetization and private deployment behind cloud-hosted agent interfaces, giving providers incentives to keep high-value skills proprietary. Yet hiding the artifacts does not conceal their behavioral effects, which remain observable in execution trajectories and form a behavioral side channel. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of identifying proprietary skills used by agents, by analyzing their execution trajectories. The researchers built a system to infer these skills, showing that hiding the artifacts of skills does not conceal their behavioral effects. The result is a method to reconstruct proprietary skills from observable trajectories.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud-hosted agent interfaces, this flags a risk: if your organization uses proprietary agent skills, check your execution trajectories for potential skill leakage immediately. Review your security measures to prevent unauthorized reconstruction of your high-value skills. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to those managing agent-based systems.

case_studies.title: LLM4OSC: Profile-Bound Natural Language Control with Deterministic Validation for Open Sound Control
case_studies.abstract: Open Sound Control (OSC) is the dominant wire protocol for real-time parametric control in professional audio, live performance, and virtual production. Large language models can emit plausible OSC, but they hallucinate addresses, mishandle type tags, and fail under paraphrase- unacceptable in show-critical contexts. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language models generating incorrect Open Sound Control commands, by building a system called LLM4OSC that validates and encodes the commands before sending them. The result is a more reliable and show-critical control system for professional audio and live performance. This is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.title: MemLens: A Value-Aware Memory Management System with Interactive Analytics for LLM-based Agents
case_studies.abstract: Recently, memory management has become a key infrastructure for LLM-based agents, as it directly affects long-horizon reasoning, personalized responses, and knowledge reuse. However, existing LLM memory systems typically adopt a coarse-grained (utility-agnostic) manner that treats heterogeneous user-LLM interaction records uniformly, leading to redundant and low-impact records persisting in the memory repository. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inefficient memory management in LLM-based agents by building a value-aware memory management system called MemLens. MemLens provides interactive analytics to manage memory records, resulting in more efficient use of memory. This is relevant for organizations using large language models.

case_studies.title: Distributing Security Controls Through Harness Engineering
case_studies.abstract: AI coding agents are being adopted at historic speed, yet security and risk concerns remain the primary barrier to scaling agentic AI across organizations. Existing security controls for coding agents are not systematically distributed to engineering teams, and vendor-native solutions introduce ecosystem dependencies that may not suit every deployment context. This paper investigates whether off-the-shelf security controls can be implemented on commercial AI coding agents and scaled to a distributed user base via a custom agent harness. A phased testing methodology was applied across four agen
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of scaling AI coding agents securely across organizations by investigating the use of off-the-shelf security controls. The authors built a custom agent harness to distribute these security controls to engineering teams. The result shows that existing security controls can be implemented on commercial AI coding agents and scaled to a distributed user base.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI coding agents, here is what to do: assess your current security controls, consider implementing off-the-shelf security controls, and evaluate the use of a custom agent harness to distribute these controls to your engineering teams. This flags a risk: if your organization uses AI coding agents without distributed security controls, check your security vulnerabilities immediately. This is directly applicable to IT infrastructure work related to AI coding agents.

case_studies.title: RepoReasoner: Evaluating Repository-Level Code Reasoning Ability of Long-Context Language Models
case_studies.abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on software engineering tasks, yet most existing benchmarks evaluate code reasoning at the function level, where all relevant information is localized. This setting fails to reflect real-world development, which requires reasoning across multiple files and complex dependency structures. We introduce RepoReasoner, a benchmark for evaluating repository-level code reasoning. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating code reasoning in large language models at a repository level, where they built a benchmark called RepoReasoner to assess code reasoning across multiple files. The result shows the ability of language models to predict output and call chains in complex codebases. This research is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.title: Detecting Knowledge Inconsistencies Across Text, Tables, and Knowledge Graphs
case_studies.abstract: Wikipedia and Wikidata are widely used for information access, LLM pre-training, and retrieval-augmented generation. Their knowledge is deeply connected but scattered across text, tables, and knowledge graphs. This raises a practical question: when these modalities disagree, how can we detect and explain the conflict? We study this problem as \emph{modality-level inconsistency detection}. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of detecting inconsistencies across different types of data, such as text, tables, and knowledge graphs, by building a system called Kontras. The result is a taxonomy of inconsistencies and a method to detect and explain conflicts. This is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: Is ChatGPT as reliable as individual reviewers assessing the quality of published journal articles from PDFs or titles and abstracts?
case_studies.abstract: Whilst Large Language Models (LLMs) have a weak to moderate ability to score published journal articles for research quality, they have not been compared with individual expert reviewers. It is also unknown whether quality scores from ChatGPT based on PDFs can improve on those from titles and abstracts through a deeper evaluation. case_studies.summary: This research compares the reliability of ChatGPT with individual expert reviewers in assessing the quality of published journal articles. case_studies.title: \textsc{IH-Benchmark}: A Conflict-Centered Benchmark for Instruction-Hierarchy Robustness in LLM Applications
case_studies.abstract: When a language model receives conflicting instructions from different priority levels, which one does it actually follow? This question lies at the heart of reliable LLM deployment. Existing benchmarks answer this only partially, often focusing on a single hierarchy edge or adapting public datasets with limited tool-use coverage. We present IH-Benchmark, a conflict-centered benchmark for instruction-hierarchy robustness across direct system-user conflicts (S>U) and tool-mediated user-tool (U>T) conflicts. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of language models receiving conflicting instructions from different priority levels, by building a benchmark called IH-Benchmark to test instruction-hierarchy robustness. The result is a more comprehensive understanding of how language models handle conflicts. This is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.title: CHARM: A Multimodal Graph Foundation Model with Hierarchical Context Modeling for Zero-Shot Transfer
case_studies.abstract: Graph foundation models (GFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for transferring knowledge across graph domains and tasks. Real-world graphs associate nodes with text, images, and other modalities, making multimodal graphs essential for representing complex entities and relations. Moreover, collecting labels and adapting models for every new graph domain is costly and often infeasible, motivating zero-shot transfer. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of transferring knowledge across different graph domains and tasks without requiring labels or adaptation, by building a multimodal graph foundation model called CHARM. The result is a model that can perform zero-shot transfer on multimodal graphs, which is useful for representing complex entities and relations. This does not directly affect IT infrastructure management work.

case_studies.title: From Role Prompt to Infinite Thinking: Exploiting Persona Conditioning for Inference Cost Attacks in LLMs
case_studies.abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, making inference efficiency and service reliability critical concerns due to their substantial computational costs. However, the autoregressive generation mechanism of LLMs enables malicious prompts to manipulate generation behaviors, inducing excessive token generation that amplifies computational consumption and threatens service efficiency. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) being vulnerable to inference cost attacks, which can make them use more computing power than needed. The researchers built a way to exploit this weakness using persona conditioning. The result shows that LLMs can be manipulated to use excessive computing power, which can affect their efficiency and reliability.
